What is this “device” doing?

It is a teaching model of an access-control gate between network services. Groups are security labels, not messaging devices. Individual VNFs send requests to each other. Source identifies where the information originates; Destination identifies the application that ultimately receives it.

A working network gives a request a route. A security rule decides whether the connection may continue. This lab focuses on that second check.

Follow a request from its sender through the two checks.

Source / Destination are explanatory application or host roles associated with the VNFs, not two additional required servers or measured network hops from the paper. The moving dot is the packet/request, not a server.

Illustration uses the default rule: same group allowed, different groups blocked. A network path is assumed; routing and message payloads are not simulated. This explanation does not change your active policy or experiment counts.

Academic review / Research context
INCS 775 · NYIT Vancouver
Fall 2022 · Group L · Xuemin Jia and Yanqing Li
Original paper: Pattaranantakul, Tseng, He, Zhang and Meddahi (2017). Academic review and presentation: Group L. Animated visualization and interactive portfolio extension: Yanqing Li, with AI assistance.
Research sources, credits and simulation limits
Research / Sources and limits
From academic review to interactive understanding
Research problem
NFV orchestrators manage deployment and lifecycle, but the reviewed work identifies a gap in specifying and enforcing fine-grained security policies alongside virtualized network services.
Proposed architecture
The original authors extend TOSCA service templates with security attributes and use a Moon-based security orchestrator, parser, client, and network hooks to support access control.
Illustrative use case
Six VNFs are partitioned into SP1 (VNF1–3) and SP2 (VNF4–6). Same-group communication is allowed, while cross-group requests are rejected under the demonstrated policy.
What this lab adds
Interactive topology, animated authorization traces, editable policy JSON, side-by-side graph comparison, deterministic batch evaluations, and exportable simulated audit data.
Research limitations
Results are logical outcomes of a simplified model, not measured latency, throughput, packet loss, real policy-engine performance, or validation against an OpenStack environment.
Future experiments
Connect to a testbed, compare policy evaluation overhead, assess dynamic rule updates, measure request latency, and validate behavior against a real enforcement implementation.
Source: Pattaranantakul, M., Tseng, Y., He, R., Zhang, Z., & Meddahi, A. (2017). A First Step Towards Security Extension for NFV Orchestrator. DOI: 10.1145/3040992.3040995. Source materials: 775 Group L A First Step Towards Security Paper Summary.pdf, pp. 1–3; 775 Group_L ppt A First Step Towards Security.pdf, slides 7–16. Academic review: INCS 775, NYIT Vancouver, Group L (2022), Xuemin Jia and Yanqing Li. Portfolio simulation and visualization: Yanqing Li.
